en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Marks of the Hundred Merits, translated by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Universal Wondrous Palace in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, seated upon a jewel...

He sat upon a magnificently adorned lion throne together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, surrounded by a countless multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, paying respectful homage, gazed up at his venerable countenance with bodies and minds unmoving.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, within the great assembly, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!

The faculties, natures, and dispositions of all sentient beings differ, and their inclinations and desires vary; yet the Tathāgata, with a single voice, expounds the Dharma according to each type, so that all these infinite varieties receive benefit.
These spoken sounds of the Great Dharma as described are all accomplished through the merit of the Tathāgata.
What is called the "merit of the Tathāgata"?
What is the measure of that which is termed "merit"?
“I only pray that you will explain its meaning for me, so as to benefit countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!
You have already transcended the stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, for you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning with great wisdom and great compassion.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to practice the ten paths of wholesome action; if the merit from all these deeds were gathered into a single mass and multiplied a hundred thousand times over, it would constitute the measure of the merit of a single universal monarch (cakravartin).
Mañjuśrī! A wheel-turning sage king accomplishes the seven treasures and is endowed with a thousand sons.
What are the seven treasures?

First is the precious golden wheel, second the precious elephant, third the precious horse, fourth the precious jewel, fifth the precious woman, sixth the precious steward, and seventh the precious general.
His thousand sons are all handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing enemies.
Such is the merit possessed by a wheel-turning sage king, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the four continents were each to achieve the merit possessed by a universal monarch (cakravartin); when such merit is accumulated to a hundred thousandfold, it constitutes the measure of the merit of a single Śakra.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in the four continents were each to achieve the same amount of merit as Śakra; if such an accumulation were multiplied a hundred thousand times, it would constitute the measure of the merit of one sixth-heavens king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in the four continents were each to achieve the merit of a Māra king; if such merit were accumulated to a hundred-thousandfold, it would constitute the measure of the merit of a Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna, the lord of a small thousand-world system.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in a small thousand-world system were each to achieve the merit possessed by a Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna; if such merit were accumulated to a hundred-thousandfold, it would constitute the measure of the merit of a Brahmā King of the Second Dhyāna who is the lord of a medium thousand-world system.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in a medium chiliocosm were each to achieve the merit possessed by a Brahmā king of the second dhyāna; if such quantities were accumulated to a full hundred-thousandfold, they would constitute the measure of merit of Mahesvara, a Brahmā king of the fourth dhyāna who is the lord of a trichiliocosm.
Mañjuśrī! Maheśvara possesses great merit, great wisdom, and great majestic power; he has achieved these through no small roots of goodness.

Why is this? Just as when the kalpa has been consumed by fire and is about to be re-established, a great rain falls upon the fourth dhyāna for five intermediate kalpas; the water accumulates until it fills the trichiliocosm, rising as high as the Brahma-world, and Maheśvara is able to know every single drop of that rain.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were each to achieve the same amount of merit as Maheśvara; if such a quantity were accumulated to a hundred thousand times its original measure, it would constitute the magnitude of the merit of a single, solitary Pratyekabuddha.
Mañjuśrī! Let us set aside this trichiliocosm for a moment.

Suppose all sentient beings in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions were each to achieve the merit possessed by a pratyekabuddha; if such quantities were accumulated to the extent of immeasurable, boundless billions of hundreds of thousands of times, they would constitute the measure of the merit of a bodhisattva in his final birth.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose a bodhisattva in his final existence and all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space in the ten directions—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether with form or formless, with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all such beings were each to achieve the same measure of merit as that possessed by this bodhisattva in his final existence. If one were to multiply such accumulations until they reached immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of times, that would constitute the measure of merit contained within a single pore of a Tathāgata’s body.”
Mañjuśrī! You should know that the pores of the Tathāgata’s body number exactly nine thousand nine hundred million; each one is endowed with immeasurable merit and virtue, as described above.

Mañjuśrī! All the merit contained within each and every pore of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas—even when multiplied by immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions—constitutes the merit of a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana) of a Tathāgata’s body.
Mañjuśrī! Thus, regarding all the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) of the Buddha’s body, briefly stated, their number is eighty kinds:
first, the uṣṇīṣa is high and prominent, such that no one can see its crown.
Second, his nose is high, long, and straight, with nostrils that do not protrude;
third, his eyebrows are like the crescent moon and are deep blue-black in color;
fourth, the lobes of his ears are well-formed.
Fifth, his body is as firm as that of Nārāyaṇa;
sixth, his bones and joints are linked together like hooks and chains;
seventh, when he walks, he remains four inches above the ground, and the marks of his footprints are perfectly formed.
Eighth, his body turns like that of an elephant king;
ninth, his nails are like red copper, thin and lustrous;
tenth, his kneecaps are perfectly rounded and beautiful.
Eleventh, the body is always fresh and clean;
twelfth, the skin and limbs are soft and supple;
thirteenth, the body is upright and straight.
Fourteenth, his fingers are slender and long;
fifteenth, the patterns on his fingers are majestic and beautiful;
sixteenth, his sinews and veins are hidden and inconspicuous.
Seventeenth, his bodily complexion is moist and beautiful;
eighteenth, his ankles are not prominent;
nineteenth, his body is not crooked.
Twentieth, his physical marks are perfectly complete;
twenty-first, his consciousness is pure;
twenty-second, his deportment is fully perfected.
Twenty-third, his dwelling place is secure and cannot be shaken;
twenty-fourth, his majestic power awes all;
twenty-fifth, sentient beings delight in seeing him.
Twenty-sixth, his face is neither narrow nor long;
twenty-seventh, his complexion is untroubled;
twenty-eighth, his countenance is beautiful and broad.
Twenty-ninth, the color of his lips is like that of the *bimba* fruit;
thirtieth, his voice is deep and far-reaching;
thirty-first, his navel is deep, round, and beautiful.
Thirty-second: the navel is coiled to the right;
thirty-third: the hands and feet are perfectly rounded;
thirty-fourth: the hands and feet are formed from the heart.
Thirty-fifth, the lines on his hands and feet are clear and penetrating;
thirty-sixth, the lines on his hands and feet are unbroken;
thirty-seventh, the light of his hands and feet possesses five colors.
Thirty-eighth, all sentient beings who see him are filled with joy;
thirty-ninth, his face is like the full moon;
fortieth, he speaks first, anticipating the thoughts of others.
Forty-first, his pores emit unsurpassed fragrance;
forty-second, the soles of his feet are level and full;
forty-third, his majestic bearing is like that of a lion king.
Forty-fourth, his advancing and halting are like those of an elephant king;
forty-fifth, his gait is like that of a swan king;
forty-sixth, his head is like a *mātuluṅga* fruit.
Forty-seventh, his body is exceedingly upright and handsome;
forty-eighth, he is fully endowed with all vocal characteristics;
forty-ninth, his canine teeth are sharp, fresh, and white.
Fifty: the color of his tongue is like red copper;
fifty-one: his tongue is thin and long;
fifty-two: his sense faculties are pure.
Fifty-third, his body is radiant and pure;
fifty-fourth, his hands and feet are moist and lustrous;
fifty-fifth, his hands and feet possess the marks of virtue.
Fifty-sixth, he is endowed with the mark of the face-gate;
fifty-seventh, the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are like red lotuses;
fifty-eighth, his abdomen is not protruding.
Fifty-ninth: the navel does not protrude;
sixtieth: the waist is slender in proportion to the body;
sixty-first: the body hairs point upward.
Sixty-second: his body is dignified and grave;
sixty-third: on his chest there is the mark of śrīvatsa; sixty-fourth:
his physical proportions are vast and magnificent.
Sixty-fifth, his hands and feet are soft and supple;
sixty-sixth, he has a halo extending one fathom;
sixty-seventh, his body is constantly illuminated by light.
Sixty-eighth, viewing all sentient beings with equanimity;
sixty-ninth, not disparaging sentient beings;
seventieth, responding to the voices of sentient beings without adding or subtracting;
Seventy-first: preaching the Dharma without attachment;
seventy-second: a single voice pervading everywhere, conforming to the speech of all sentient beings;
seventy-third: preaching the Dharma with causes and conditions.
Seventy-fourth: No sentient being is able to fully observe them;
seventy-fifth: His movements are clockwise;
seventy-sixth: He has no expression of anger.
Seventy-seventh: his hair is long and beautiful;
seventy-eighth: his hair is not disheveled;
seventy-ninth: his hair curls to the right.
The eighty [minor marks] include having hair that is deep blue-black. "Mañjuśrī!
As described above, these are called the secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana) of the Tathāgata."

When the accumulation of merit has reached a full measure of immeasurable, boundless billions of hundreds of thousands of times, it constitutes the amount of merit for a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) of the Tathāgata’s body.
Of these secondary marks, there are eighty:
the first is the likeness of a Brahmā king;...
Second, an image of Śakra;
third, an image of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
fourth, an image of Virūḍhaka; and fifth, an image of Virūpākṣa.
Fifth, an image of Virūpākṣa;
sixth, an image of Vaiśravaṇa;
seventh, an image of Varuṇa.
Eighth, an image of the Sun Deity;
ninth, an image of the Moon Deity;
tenth, an image of the Fire Deity.
Eleventh, the image of a Vāyu-deva;
twelfth, the image of a Nāga-rāja;
thirteenth, the image of a Ṛṣi.
Fourteenth, the image of a young boy;
fifteenth, the image of a young girl;
sixteenth, the image of the seat of the noble sages.
Seventeenth, the image of a jeweled banner;
eighteenth, the image of a bull king;
nineteenth, the image of the goddess Puṇyavatī.
The twentieth is the image of the King of Mountains;
the twenty-first is the image of the Makara Great Fish;
the twenty-second is the image of the King of the Golden-Winged Birds.
Twenty-third, the image of King Vyāghra;
twenty-fourth, the image of King Aśva;
twenty-fifth, the image of King Mayūra.
Twenty-sixth, the image of the *jīvamjīvaka* bird;
twenty-seventh, the image of the *kalaviṅka*;
twenty-eighth, the image of the *śukapattra*.
Twenty-ninth is the image of a parrot;
thirtieth is the image of a *cātaka* bird;
thirty-first is the image of a king of geese.
Thirty-second, the image of a dove;
thirty-third, the image of an elephant king;
thirty-fourth, the image of a palace.
Thirty-fifth is the image of a maṇi jewel;
thirty-sixth is the image of a necklace;
thirty-seventh is the image of the great ocean.
Thirty-eighth is the image of a lotus flower;
thirty-ninth is the image of Nandabhadra;
fortieth is the image of a bathing pool.
Forty-first is the image of the divine *darbha* grass;
forty-second is the image of *sṛṣṭika*;
forty-third is the image of the flower garland.
Forty-fourth is the image of the jeweled crown;
forty-fifth is the image of Śrīvasa;
forty-sixth is the image of the parasol.
Forty-seventh, the image of a river;
forty-eighth, the image of a cloud in the sky;
forty-ninth, the image of a precious sword.
Fifty: the image of a long hook;
fifty-one: the image of a *bimba* fruit tree;
fifty-two: the image of a finger ring.
Fifty-third, the image of an ear-ornament;
fifty-fourth, the image of a vajra;
fifty-fifth, the image of a spear and halberd.
Fifty-sixth, the image of a spear;
fifty-seventh, the image of a long sword;
fifty-eighth, the image of a battle discus.
Fifty-ninth, the image of a bow and arrow;
sixtieth, the image of a battle-axe;
sixty-first, the image of a lasso.
Sixty-second is the image of a plow;
sixty-third is the image of medicinal herbs;
sixty-fourth is the image of a milch cow.
Sixty-fifth is the image of a wild buffalo;
sixty-sixth is the image of a horned goat;
sixty-seventh is the image of a white fly-whisk.
Sixty-eighth, the image of a celestial drum;
sixty-ninth, the image of a golden mallet;
seventieth, the image of a conch shell.
Seventy-first is the image of a precious mirror;
seventy-second is the image of a great tortoise;
seventy-third is the image of a plowshare blade.
Seventy-fourth, the image of a flower vase;
seventy-fifth, the image of powdered rice;
seventy-sixth, the image of a flowering tree.
Seventy-seventh is the image of a fruit tree;
seventy-eighth is the image of a king of geese;
seventy-ninth is the image of a lion within a wheel.
The eightieth is the mark of the deer-king. "Mañjuśrī!
As described above, these are called the merits of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks."
When the accumulated number reaches a full measure of immeasurable, boundless billions of hundreds of thousands, they combine to form a single mark of the Tathāgata’s body.
There are thirty-two such marks of the Tathāgata’s body:
the first is that the soles of his feet are level and firm.
Second, his hands and feet have wheels with a thousand spokes and rims;
third, his fingers and toes are slender and long;
fourth, his hands and feet are as soft as tūla-cotton.
Fifth, the heels are full and well-formed;
sixth, the fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane;
seventh, the insteps are high and level, in proportion to the heels.
Eighth, his calves are rounded and long like those of the Eṇeya deer king;
ninth, when standing upright with his body straight, his hands hang down past his knees;
tenth, his male organ is concealed and not visible.
Eleventh, his body is equal in height and breadth, like a nyagrodha tree;
twelfth, a single hair grows from each pore;
thirteenth, the hairs of his body point upward, are blue-black in color, soft, and curl to the right.
Fourteenth, his physical complexion is subtle and exquisite, surpassing Jambūnada gold;
fifteenth, his bodily radiance extends for ten feet;
sixteenth, his skin is thin, fine, and smooth, such that it does not retain dust or grime.
Seventeenth, his two shoulders are rounded and well-formed;
eighteenth, his body is broad and upright;
nineteenth, his chest is like that of a lion king.
Twentieth: the areas beneath both armpits are full;
twenty-first: the teeth are white and large;
twenty-second: there are forty teeth.
Twenty-third: His teeth are white, even, closely set, and deeply rooted;
twenty-fourth: He is fully endowed in seven places;
twenty-fifth: His jaw is square like that of a lion king.
Twenty-sixth: among all tastes, he attains the supreme taste, and from two places within his throat, streams of saliva flow forth;
twenty-seventh: his tongue is soft and thin, capable of covering his face up to the hairline;
twenty-eighth: his Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
Twenty-ninth, his eyes are like the *utpala* lotus;
thirtieth, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king;
thirty-first, the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows is the color of white jade or snow.
The thirty-second is the protuberance on the crown of the head formed of flesh and bone. "Mañjuśrī!
These that have been thus described are called the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata."

All these accumulated merits, numbering fully as many as there are immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, unmeasurable, inconceivable, and unspeakable multiples, combine to form the Great Dharma-speech and voice of the Tathāgata.

Mañjuśrī! In this way, the great Dharma speech and sounds of all Buddhas are able to reach the diverse inclinations of all sentient beings throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds, teaching and transforming them by expounding the Dharma according to their respective capacities for understanding.
Mañjuśrī! All the speech and sounds of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with such immeasurable merits; that they universally benefit sentient beings throughout the world is likewise so.
Mañjuśrī! The measure of merit as described above is inconceivable; it is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?

Such merit arises from generosity, morality, and cultivation, as well as from the various virtues of great compassion, great wisdom, and the power of skillful means; therefore, it is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Mañjuśrī! There are two kinds of dharmas that give rise to the body of a Tathāgata. What are these two?
First is the power of supreme vows, and second is the power of skillful means.
By means of these two dharmas, the body of a Tathāgata is produced;
even his voice, marks and signs, preaching of the Dharma, and conduct are all accomplished through these two causes.

Mañjuśrī! It is because the Tathāgata wishes to have compassion for, benefit, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings that he appears in the world. Since sentient beings possess various dispositions and their inclinations differ, the Tathāgata manifests diverse forms according to those distinctions, preaching the Dharma to teach and transform them, and showing them their respective practices so that they may enter the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, having heard the various merits spoken by the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have now attained great and excellent benefit.”
One is able to know that the Tathāgata is the unequaled among equals, the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, who acts as the great refuge for all sentient beings, pure and untainted like space.
"It is most rare for me to have encountered this now.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the others, along with all the bhikṣus, joined their palms, received it with faith, and joyfully put it into practice.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Marks of the Hundredfold Merits.
